nameStory: The elm borer gets its straightforward name from its lifestyle - it's a beetle that bores into elm trees! The larvae tunnel through the wood of American and slippery elms, creating galleries beneath the bark where they feed and grow. This boring behavior is so characteristic that it earned the beetle its common name.
description: The elm borer is a longhorn beetle that spends its larval stage tunneling through elm trees. Like other longhorn beetles, adults have notably long antennae that can be as long as or longer than their body. These beetles are wood-borers, meaning their young develop inside living trees rather than in dead wood like many other beetles. Unfortunately, they can weaken elm trees and spread Dutch elm disease as they move from tree to tree.

idTips.label: Long antennae
idTips.description: Antennae are distinctively long - often as long as the beetle's body or longer, feeling thin and segmented when gently touched

idTips.label: Cylindrical body
idTips.description: Body is elongated and somewhat cylindrical, feeling firm and smooth to the touch

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized beetle, roughly the length of your thumbnail when fully grown

idTips.label: Host trees
idTips.description: Found exclusively on or near American elm and slippery elm trees

idTips.label: Exit holes
idTips.description: Look for small, round holes in elm bark where adults have emerged - about the size of a pencil lead

habitat: You'll find elm borers wherever American elm and slippery elm trees grow in New England - along rivers and streams, in rich bottomland soils, and in parks or neighborhoods where elms have been planted. They prefer areas with moisture since elms thrive in these conditions. Look for them in lowland areas, floodplains, and urban settings where elm trees are present.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging from trees and may be seen crawling on elm bark. This is when mating occurs and females seek out suitable elm trees for egg-laying.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period for adults - they're most likely to be spotted on elm trees during warm days. Fresh exit holes may appear in bark as new adults emerge.
seasonality.fall: Adult activity decreases as temperatures drop. Larvae are developing inside elm trees but aren't visible from outside.
seasonality.winter: Adults are inactive and larvae continue developing slowly inside the protection of elm bark and wood.

funFact: Elm borers are unwitting accomplices in one of North America's greatest ecological disasters - they carry the fungus that causes Dutch elm disease on their bodies as they tunnel from tree to tree, helping spread the disease that has killed millions of elm trees across the continent!
confusionNotes: Elm borers can be confused with their close relative, the round-headed apple tree borer, which is similar in size and shape. The key difference is their host plants - if you find the beetle on an elm tree, it's likely an elm borer, but if it's on apple, hawthorn, or other fruit trees, it's probably the apple tree borer.
contextualKnowledge: While elm borers are native insects that historically had a balanced relationship with elm trees, the introduction of Dutch elm disease from Europe has made their role more problematic. They've become vectors for this non-native fungal disease, turning them from minor tree pests into major contributors to elm decline.
compareHints: Compared to its closest relative in the same genus, the round-headed apple tree borer, the elm borer is distinguished primarily by its host tree preference - elm borers stick exclusively to elm species while apple tree borers prefer fruit trees and related plants in the rose family. Both have the characteristic long antennae of longhorn beetles, but their different host plants make identification straightforward in the field.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its relative the Elm Borer which targets elm trees and has a more elongated head, the Round-headed Apple Tree Borer has that distinctly rounded head and sticks to fruit trees.
